description:
Meet Nativ-1

A multidisciplinary team in data science, systems engineering, and mechatronics focused on space exploration. We cross-reference Earth, Moon, and Mars data to identify terrestrial environments for simulating future interplanetary missions.
summary: Nativ-1 is an interactive tool that finds places on Earth whose terrain looks most like chosen landing sites on the Moon and Mars, with a focus on lesser-studied sites in Argentina, Peru, Colombia and Mexico instead of the classic Atacama, Hawaii, Iceland or Antarctica. We compared the multi-scale slope relief of 13 Earth sites (10 candidates plus 3 classic reference sites: Namib, Erg Chebbi and Lake Gairdner) against 4 lunar and 3 Martian reference sites, using NASA elevation data (LOLA for the Moon, MOLA for Mars) and the Copernicus DEM for Earth. The ranking is a probability, not an invented score: it is the chance (%) that a site lands in the top 3 most similar once uncertain weights and measurement error are accounted for (SMAA-2). Every result also states where the analogy breaks down (gravity, vacuum, thin atmosphere, radiation) and which mission test the site is suited for. This matters because testing landers, rovers and habitats on Earth is far cheaper than in space, but only if the test site is honestly characterized.
details:
Nativ-1 ranks Earth sites by how similar their terrain is to a Moon or Mars reference site, and shows the result on an interactive map/globe. MOON (about 70% of our effort) and MARS (about 30%) are computed and shown separately. For each reference site the user sees a Top-K list of Earth sites, the probability of each being among the 3 most similar, how robust that is to measurement error, and a plain-language explanation: strongest matches, where the analogy breaks down, and which mission test it is useful for (e.g., landing slope < 10°, rover slope ≤ 15°).

How it works.

  1. For every site we read a window of the elevation model remotely (no bulk downloads) and compute slope at 4 spatial scales. Earth is always degraded to the resolution of the planetary body (118 m for the Moon, 463 m for Mars), never the other way around.
  2. We compare the slope distributions of each Earth site with each reference using the Wasserstein-1 distance (in degrees).
  3. We rank with SMAA-2 (10,000 draws of unknown weights, 200 replicas of measurement noise). This avoids made-up weights and gives a probability of being in the top 3 plus a robustness label ("robust" or "sensitive to measurement error").
  4. We validated the metric on 9 documented lunar terrain sites (5 maria, 4 highlands) with two predictions frozen before running. P1 (each site's nearest neighbour is of its own terrain class) was met; P2 (maria and highlands separate more at 3186 m than at 118 m) was not met. This shows the metric distinguishes lunar terrains; it does NOT validate the Earth-to-planet comparison, since published Earth-planet pairs for our sites do not exist.
  5. Thermal inertia, mineralogy and hillshade images are shown as descriptive context only, outside the ranking, because they are not measured in comparable units across Earth, Moon and Mars.

Example results (relief only; probability of being in the top 3 among all Earth sites). Apollo 15: Puna–Antofalla (100%), La Payunia (100%), Andahua (97%). Apollo 17: Andahua, Puna–Antofalla and La Payunia (all 100%). Aristarchus: La Payunia and Puna–Antofalla (100%), then the classic Namib site (59%). Mare Tranquillitatis: Erg Chebbi (100%, classic site), Salinas Grandes (99.9%, flagged sensitive to measurement error: these flat sites are at the noise level), Lake Gairdner (94%). Mars, Jezero: Alta Guajira (95%), La Payunia (91%), Namib (60%). Gale: Carachi Pampa and Puna–Antofalla (100%), Piedra Pómez (84%). Meridiani: Sechura, Lake Gairdner and Erg Chebbi (100%). Tatacoa (Colombia) is excluded from Mars by an aridity index of 1.1 (sub-humid).

Scientific honesty. No Earth site reproduces everything. We only claim "most similar in the measured relief", never "the best analog". Mars is limited to arid, hyper-arid and semi-arid bare-soil terrain (no glaciers, liquid water, dense vegetation or active hydrothermal systems). Known limits: polar sites (e.g., Shackleton) are not supported; Mars landing/mobility requirements are at metre scale and cannot be evaluated with 463 m slopes.

Benefits. Mission teams get a transparent, reproducible shortlist of low-cost test sites; under-studied Latin American sites gain visibility; every claim is traceable to a source (requisitos.csv) in this case.

What we hope to achieve. A starting point for choosing field-test sites for future lunar bases and Mars missions, extensible to more sites, finer-resolution data and additional dimensions as comparable measurements become available.

Tools. Python 3.14 (rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, pandas, Pillow, requests, pyarrow, pyhdf, earthaccess); SMAA-2 and the Wasserstein-1 distance implemented in our own code (smaa.py, distributions.py); web app built with Vite, React 19, TypeScript, MapLibre GL, three.js and Tailwind CSS, configured as a static site for Netlify (netlify.toml).
